scan.summary: This is your written plan for what employees do in a fire, chemical release, medical emergency or earthquake at the Portland facility. It is your own document, so you can fix it. In Oregon it is checked against Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule, OAR 437-002-0042. It covers evacuation, headcounts, first aid, alarm signals, designated wardens and reviews with employees. It leaves out three things the rule requires: how to report an emergency, how to shut down critical equipment before leaving, and who employees contact about the plan. It was last revised in February 2021 and shows no review since.
scan.freshness_note: The cover page says 'Revised February 2021', so the plan is about 5 years and 8 months old. Section 6 says the facilities lead reviews it every January, but nothing in the file shows the reviews for 2022 to 2026 happened. Ask whether there is a newer version or a record of those January reviews. If there isn't, re-date it when you add the missing sections below.

gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
gaps.description: The plan says pull stations are at each exit and that an outside company monitors the alarm. It never says who calls 911, how to report a chemical release or medical emergency that won't set off the fire alarm, or which phone numbers to use.
gaps.fix: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. It should say: pull the nearest station for a fire; call 911 from a safe place for any fire, release or serious injury; tell the incident coordinator or a supervisor; and give the site address to give the dispatcher. List the internal phone numbers.
gaps.locator: not in the document (would belong in Section 2 or a new section before Section 3)
gaps.quote: Manual pull stations are located at each exit door.

gaps.title: No procedure for shutting down critical equipment before evacuating
gaps.description: The rule requires procedures for emergency operation or shutdown of critical equipment before evacuation. The plan tells everyone to leave at once. The only shutdown it mentions is the ventilation shutoff during shelter-in-place. For a chemical manufacturer with a laboratory, there is nothing on reactors, heating, transfer pumps, gas cylinders or other process equipment, and nothing saying who, if anyone, stays behind to do it.
gaps.fix: Decide which equipment must be made safe before people leave. Name the job title responsible, write the steps and a cut-off point after which that person leaves too. If nothing needs a shutdown, say so in writing.
gaps.quote: all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit

gaps.title: No named contact for questions about the plan; incident coordinator not identified
gaps.description: The rule requires the names or job titles of the people employees can contact for more information about their duties under the plan. No one is named for this. The plan also relies on an 'incident coordinator' but never says who holds that role or who stands in when that person is absent.
gaps.fix: Add a contacts section. Give the job title, and ideally the name and phone number, of the plan contact (for example the facilities lead), the incident coordinator and a backup.
gaps.locator: not in the document (Section 4 refers to the incident coordinator without naming the role holder)
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point

gaps.title: Earthquake listed in scope but no earthquake procedure
gaps.description: Section 1 lists earthquakes as a covered emergency. The plan only gives procedures for alarm-triggered evacuation and shelter-in-place. It doesn't say what to do during and right after shaking (drop, cover and hold on, then evacuate once shaking stops and check for chemical spills). The rule asks for the 'type of evacuation' for each emergency. Whether that means a separate earthquake procedure is required is my reading, not a checked requirement.
gaps.fix: Add a short earthquake procedure. Cover what to do during shaking, when to evacuate, which routes to avoid (the freight lift, racking, the lab), and a post-quake check for chemical spills and gas leaks.
gaps.quote: a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility

gaps.title: No statement on how far employees respond to chemical spills
gaps.description: The plan covers chemical releases by evacuating or sheltering in place. It doesn't say whether employees clean up small spills themselves (incidental releases) or never respond. If employees do respond beyond small incidental spills, the federal hazardous waste and emergency response rule (HAZWOPER, 29 CFR 1910.120(q)) would require a separate emergency response plan and training. I'm not sure how Oregon has adopted this; I believe it is by reference.
gaps.fix: Add a sentence saying employees do not respond to chemical releases beyond small incidental spills they are trained to clean up, and that larger releases are handled by the fire department. If that isn't true, a separate HAZWOPER emergency response plan is needed.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.120(q) (not confirmed for how Oregon applies it)
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds.

gaps.title: Appendices A and B are not in the file
gaps.description: The plan points to evacuation maps (Appendix A) and to the floor warden and first-aid responder roster (Appendix B) for exit route assignments and designated evacuation helpers. Neither is attached. So there is no way to check that exit routes are assigned or that designated employees exist, which the rule requires.
gaps.fix: Attach the current evacuation maps and the current warden and first-aid roster to the plan, with dates. Check that the roster names people who still work there.
gaps.quote: Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)

gaps.title: The plan's own January review has not been recorded since 2021
gaps.description: The plan commits to a review every January, but the revision date is still February 2021 and there is no review log or sign-off. This is the plan's own commitment, not a specific Oregon rule.
gaps.fix: Add a review log at the end (date, reviewer, changes made). Carry out and record a review now.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January

facts.value: All employees evacuate when the fire alarm sounds; the plan gives no role for employees in fighting fires
facts.quote: When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit.
facts.affects: Under Oregon's portable fire extinguisher rule (OAR 437-002-0187), a workplace where everyone evacuates in a fire needs both an emergency action plan and a fire prevention plan.

facts.value: The Portland facility has a laboratory with laboratory staff
facts.quote: Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall.
facts.affects: May bring in OSHA's laboratory chemicals rule (29 CFR 1910.1450), which requires a chemical hygiene plan.

facts.quote: including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff
facts.affects: May bring in US DOT driver and hazardous materials transport rules, depending on vehicle size and what is carried.

facts.value: Fire alarm monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract
facts.quote: The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract.
facts.affects: Alarm inspection and test records from this vendor are the evidence for the alarm system requirement.

facts.value: Emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock; AED and first-aid kit in the front office
facts.quote: taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely
facts.affects: First-aid and eyewash rules (OAR 437-002-0161) may require eyewash near every place corrosives are handled, including the laboratory; the plan names only the loading dock.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
